title: Trump administration plans to widen groups of immigrants targeted for deportation, documents show
text: The Trump administration intends to instruct immigration agents to substantially broaden the categories of immigrants they target for deportation, according to two draft memos seen by Reuters and first reported on Saturday by the McClatchy news organization. Two sources familiar with the plans told Reuters that Secretary of Homeland Security John Kelly has approved the documents, which are undergoing a final review at the White House. They are expected to go out to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection (CBP) early next week. Under the orders, hundreds of thousands of people would face expedited removal proceedings, among them people who had not been prioritized for deportation under former President Barack Obama. The memos serve as guidance telling agents in the field how to carry out two executive orders Trump signed on Jan. 25, which are intended to deter future migration and drive more illegal migrants out of the United States. One memo tells ICE agents to disregard Obama's memos on immigration priorities, which targeted only recent arrivals and convicted criminal migrants for deportation. Migrants who have been charged with crimes but not convicted would instead be prioritized for deportation. The guidance also gives ICE agents wide discretion over whom to deport and treats anyone in the United States illegally as subject to deportation. It does, however, leave in place Obama's 2012 executive action that protected 750,000 people brought to the United States illegally by their parents. The future of that policy, known as DACA, has been hotly debated inside the White House, according to sources familiar with the discussions. At a news conference on Friday, Trump said DACA was a “very difficult subject” for him. The ICE memo also says that immigrants will not be afforded rights under U.S. privacy laws.

title: Sex Differences in the Right Tail of Cognitive Abilities: An Update and Cross-Cultural Extension
text: Matthew C. Makel et al., October 31, 2016. Abstract: Differences between males and females in the right tail of ability (at or above the 95th percentile) have been widely discussed because of their possible role in differences in achievement and occupation among adults. This study presents updated male-female ability ratios for 320,000 7th grade students in the United States, covering the right tail (top 5%) through the extreme right tail (top 0.01%) from 2011 to 2015, based on measures of math, verbal, and science reasoning. In addition, the study establishes male-female ability ratios in the right tail for a sample of over 7000 7th grade students in India from 2011 to 2015. The results show that ratios in the extreme right tail of math ability in the U.S. have shrunk over the last 20 years (while still favoring males) and have stayed relatively stable in the verbal domain (still favoring females). Similar patterns of male-female ratios in the extreme right tail were observed in the Indian sample.

title: Trump may seek to tighten, rather than scrap, Iran nuclear deal
text: Rather than tearing up the Iran nuclear deal, the Trump administration is looking at ways to tighten enforcement and renegotiate key terms, though it may prove impossible to persuade other major powers and Iran to consider revising the agreement. Under the 2015 accord between Tehran and six world powers, Iran agreed to curb its nuclear program in return for relief from some U.S., European and U.N. economic sanctions. Many experts regard it as a success so far. This week the Trump administration signaled a tougher but ambiguous line toward Iran, putting the Islamic Republic “on notice” after an Iranian ballistic missile test and then imposing economic sanctions on 13 individuals and 12 entities on Friday. According to two sources familiar with the matter, the options under consideration include insisting that the Vienna-based International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), the U.N. nuclear watchdog, police Iran's compliance more strictly, including by demanding access to military sites. “The basic idea is that the IAEA has to be granted access,” said one source with knowledge of the matter, who acknowledged that it would be hard for the U.S. administration to win support for military site inspections from the other 34 countries on the IAEA board of governors. The two sources said the U.S. would also seek to remove “sunset” provisions from the pact, which allow some restrictions on Iran's nuclear program to begin expiring in 10 years and which critics consider the deal's biggest flaw. In addition, one of the sources said, the administration could press the agency to report more information on Iran's compliance with the nuclear pact, noting that the agency has scaled back its reporting of some data, such as how much low-enriched uranium Iran is stockpiling.

title: TV chef Vivian Howard brings hope to her rural hometown
text: Just before Christmas, in the soup kitchen that serves Kinston, North Carolina, a small town built on tobacco, textiles and hogs, the chef and cooking show star Vivian Howard finished stirring a pot of pork and sweet potato stew and turned to a local television reporter. How did it feel, the reporter asked, to know that she had saved her hometown? “If I had saved Kinston,” she replied, “we wouldn’t need a food bank, and all these people wouldn’t be waiting for lunch.” Ms. Howard, 38, has been called many things. Her mother calls her the life of the party. Her father calls her Big Time, a nickname from her childhood. A few of the 80 people she employs call her a control freak. But “hometown hero” may be the label that makes her the most uncomfortable. “Saving a town was not what I was trying to do,” she said. “I’m just a storyteller. A storyteller who cooks.” Even so, Ms. Howard, the girl who spent her childhood plotting her escape from this rural county in eastern North Carolina, has become an unlikely engine of its economic and cultural revival. Twelve years ago, when her family persuaded her to come home and open a restaurant, she felt that she had somehow failed. Now she is five seasons into “A Chef’s Life,” her popular public television show. Her restaurant, Chef the Farmer, draws talent from the best professional kitchens in the South, and traveling food celebrities stop by to learn about the region. New restaurants, galleries and a brewery have opened in town. The woman who taught her how to make biscuits can charge tourists $100 for a private lesson.

title: Will the GOP unite against Trump over his Muslim ban?
text: Less than 24 hours after President Barack Obama sought to set the tone for the nation's response to the threat of terrorism with an Oval Office address, Trump needed only a press release to cause an uproar by calling for an outright ban on Muslims entering the United States. On Tuesday morning the billionaire businessman stood defiantly by his statement, warning that failing to follow his plans would lead to another September 11-style terror attack on U.S. soil. "You're going to have many more World Trade Centers if you don't solve it -- many, many more and probably beyond the World Trade Center," Trump told CNN's Chris Cuomo in a contentious interview on "New Day." The episode is a microcosm of how the 2016 campaign has unfolded. Trump has repeatedly forced candidates, state party chairs, senators and conservative pundits to respond to his actions and remarks, however outlandish and improbable. In turn, all of them have struggled with how to handle the bombastic real estate tycoon, who has led state and national polls since the summer. Trump's lasting ability to set the terms of the debate for the GOP continues to leave party leaders worried that he will push voters toward Hillary Clinton, help down-ballot Democrats and inflict long-term damage on the Republican brand. Yet, unlike his earlier provocative statements, this one appears to have triggered a level of backlash from GOP party leaders and his rivals that could prove a tipping point in fellow Republicans' willingness to criticize him directly and openly. Jeb Bush called Trump "unhinged." Ted Cruz said it wasn't his policy.

title: Flynn admits lying about Russia contacts, agrees to cooperate with U.S. investigation
text: Michael Flynn, the former national security adviser, pleaded guilty on Friday to lying to the FBI about his contacts with Russia and agreed to cooperate with prosecutors investigating the actions of President Donald Trump's inner circle before he took office. The turn of events also raised fresh questions about whether Jared Kushner, Trump's son-in-law, played a role in those Russia contacts. Flynn became the first member of Trump's administration to plead guilty to a crime uncovered by special counsel Robert Mueller's wide-ranging investigation into Russian attempts to influence the 2016 U.S. election and possible collusion by Trump aides. Under a plea bargain, Flynn admitted in a Washington court that he lied when FBI investigators asked him about his conversations last December with Sergei Kislyak, then Russia's ambassador, just weeks before Trump took office. Prosecutors said the two men discussed U.S. sanctions against Russia and that Flynn also asked Kislyak to help delay a U.N. vote seen as damaging to Israel. On both occasions, he appeared to be undermining the policies of outgoing President Barack Obama. Prosecutors also said a “very senior member” of Trump's transition team had told Flynn to contact Russia and other foreign governments to try to influence them ahead of the U.N. vote. Sources told Reuters that the “very senior” official was Kushner, a key member of Trump's transition team who is now the president's senior adviser. Abbe Lowell, Kushner's lawyer, did not respond to multiple requests for comment. He has said previously that Kushner has voluntarily cooperated with all relevant inquiries and would continue to do so. Flynn's decision to cooperate with Mueller's team marked a major escalation in an investigation that has dogged the president since he took office in January.

title: Five Filipino hostages released by Somali pirates reunited with their families
text: Five Filipino fishermen who had been held hostage by Somali pirates for nearly five years have been reunited with their families after their release. The seafarers landed on Friday at the airport in Manila, the Philippine capital, where fisherman Arnel Balbero wept as he met his relatives at the Manila International Airport on October 28, 2016. "I am so happy. This is what I had been praying for every night," said Arnel Balbero, 33, as his four siblings hugged him at the airport. "Just to be with my family, even if we have nothing, even if we have only little to eat, I am already happy," he said. His sister, Lilia, shook at the sight of her brother. "It's like a miracle. We never lost hope he would be freed," she said. The Filipinos were among 26 hostages from Cambodia, China, Taiwan, Indonesia and Vietnam who were freed on October 22. Those 26 hostages, plus three others, made up the crew of the Naham 3, which was seized south of the Seychelles in March 2012. The captain of their Omani-flagged but Taiwanese-owned vessel died during the hijacking, and two other crew members died of illness in captivity. Balbero's cousin and fellow former hostage, Elmer, said the Somali pirates had cared little about their captives' health. "We asked the pirates for medicine but they did not give us any. Instead they said, 'Where is your money?'" said Elmer. The captives also said the pirates beat them. "In our first week, they called it our introduction. They used bamboo to beat us," Arnel said.

title: Ukraine's president denies obstructing anti-corruption work
text: Ukrainian President Petro Poroshenko on Friday denied interfering with the work of law enforcement bodies that investigate corruption, and he urged those agencies not to play politics. This week Ukrainian authorities have faced accusations of deliberately sabotaging anti-corruption reforms, a key condition for international support as the country grapples with a Russian-backed separatist insurgency. Perceived backsliding by Kiev on its reform pledges, including delays in setting up an independent court to handle corruption cases, has held up billions of dollars in loans under Ukraine's $17.5 billion IMF program. “Over the last 2.5 years of activity of the anti-corruption institutions, everybody, including the heads of these institutions, has said there has not been a single instance of interference by the president in their work,” Poroshenko said. “We consider it unacceptable when the leaders of any law enforcement bodies, including anti-corruption, begin to play in the political field,” he told a news conference during a visit to the Lithuanian capital Vilnius. “They must be independent, protected from political influence.” Moves by Ukraine's parliament and prosecutors against existing anti-corruption bodies such as the NABU investigative bureau drew a wave of criticism this week from reformers and from Kiev's foreign backers, including the IMF. Poroshenko's faction is the largest in parliament, and the president also nominates the general prosecutor. “Corrupt Empire Strikes Back,” read the headline of the English-language newspaper Kyiv Post on Friday. Christine Lagarde, the head of the International Monetary Fund, said that during a telephone conversation late on Thursday she had urged Poroshenko to speed up the fight against corruption. Lagarde said she and Poroshenko had discussed the need to protect the independence of NABU and similar institutions and had agreed that establishing an anti-corruption court was urgent.

title: U.S. retailers count on Congress, not Bolivia, to defeat Trump border tax
text: Target Corp, Wal-Mart Stores Inc and other retailers are setting aside plans to move supply bases closer to the United States in response to a possible border tax, and are instead betting on killing support for the tax idea in Congress. President Donald Trump's push for a tax on imports, such as the 20 percent levy proposed by House Republicans, could lift U.S. consumer prices by as much as 25 percent, industry officials said. Last week the President said he favored an ‘import tax’ that could be adjusted to reflect the tax rate that the country of origin applies to U.S. products. Retailers' decision to put off supply chain investment in countries such as Bolivia and Romania and concentrate on lobbying Congress shows how Trump's ambitious agenda has introduced a new level of risk to operating outside U.S. borders. But because the tax proposals are vague and may never be implemented, retail industry executives are still unwilling to change their operating infrastructure. The Retail Industry Leaders Association, which is leading the industry's lobbying effort, has held 140 meetings with lawmakers since December, focusing on the costs of a new tax and encouraging lawmakers who oppose it. Hopes for quick passage of a tax bill suffered a blow last month when the Republican attempt to overhaul the national healthcare law failed to reach a vote in the U.S. House of Representatives. Trump and Republican leaders have said they still intend to pass a healthcare reform law first, casting further doubt on when Congress may take up tax reform. The border tax proposal will likely be “as messy as the healthcare bill,” according to Brian Dodge, senior executive vice-president of public affairs for the retail lobby group.

title: Think You Can't Meditate?
text: At some point recently — maybe in the last six months, or a year — everyone I know started meditating. Or at least they started talking about wanting to meditate. Some used apps like Headspace; others just put on trippy music and zoned out. A few went to events run by Medi Club, a kind of group. “Mindfulness,” we're calling it: this urge to carve out a chunk of every day and simply live in the present. I could use some of that calm and focus. I tend either to live in paranoia about the future or to dwell on the foibles of the past. Besides, I have never met a fitness or health or beauty or wellness trend I didn't want to try. My old set of Tae Bo VHS tapes is slowly decomposing in a garage in California. Left to my own devices, meditation time becomes nap time, so I knew I needed some structure and supervision. I had heard that meditation studios are the new yoga studios, and I was intrigued. I picked Mndfl, which has locations in Greenwich Village, on the Upper East Side and in Williamsburg, Brooklyn. Most of its classes last 45 minutes, which is roughly 44 minutes longer than I have ever meditated successfully. I know 45 minutes can feel like an eternity, because I do both SoulCycle and therapy. I went to the studio on East Eighth Street on a freezing weeknight. Inside it is sleek, with blond woods and white walls, but it has a certain coziness — think free tea and an area to read — sort of like a particularly nice Airbnb. My first official foray was an hourlong sound bath led by Sara Auster, a yoga teacher and, according to her website, certified sound therapy practitioner.

title: Germany opens trial over 'Love Parade' deaths
text: Ten people went on trial in Germany on Friday over alleged failures in planning the 2010 Love Parade music festival, where 21 people were killed and more than 650 injured in a stampede. Prosecutors have charged the defendants, four employees of the company that organized the event in the industrial city of Duisburg and six from the local authority, with negligent manslaughter and bodily harm. The defendants have denied any wrongdoing in the disaster. Eight foreigners from Spain, Bosnia, the Netherlands, Australia, Italy and China were among those killed on July 24, 2010, when panic erupted in a packed underpass that was the only way into the venue for the techno music festival. The trial has been moved to a congress center in the nearby city of Duesseldorf because the court rooms in Duisburg were too small for what is expected to be one of the biggest trials in postwar Germany, involving dozens of lawyers and plaintiffs. The trial is expected to last until at least the end of next year. But the clock is ticking on the proceedings, as the statute of limitations expires in July 2020.
